problem_solved: Choose a capacity change for an overloaded stage without assuming that every shared dependency scales with it.
design_scenario: A shop adds application servers while all requests still reach one saturated shared database.
application_steps: Locate the saturated component rather than treating the whole system as one box.
Compare more resources on that component with distributing its work across instances.
Trace the shared database path and verify whether it remains the limiting stage after application scaling.
decision_or_tradeoff: A larger instance has practical capacity limits; more instances require suitable work distribution and do not automatically increase shared database capacity.
animation_reason: A static larger-machine versus multiple-machines diagram with the shared dependency highlighted is sufficient.

inquiry_evidence.quote: Checkout demand doubles. The application CPU is busy, but the database has spare capacity. What would you change first, and what evidence would make you choose a larger machine over more machines?

fundamental_evidence.quote: Managing overlapping tasks vs executing tasks at the same time.

application_evidence.quote: One cook can alternate tasks; several cooks can work simultaneously.

problem_solved: Distinguish overlapping in-progress tasks from simultaneous execution when trying to remove waiting or add compute capacity.
design_scenario: A product page makes independent remote calls; overlapping their waits differs from running CPU work on several cores.
application_steps: Identify which tasks are independent and which depend on earlier results.
Overlap independent remote waits where appropriate, while bounding in-flight work.
For CPU work, determine whether simultaneous execution and available cores actually provide extra capacity.
Measure the critical path and throughput instead of equating more in-progress requests with faster completion.
decision_or_tradeoff: Concurrency can hide waiting without adding simultaneous CPU execution; excess in-flight work can overload dependencies.
animation_reason: A single-worker interleaving timeline versus multiple workers executing simultaneously exposes the distinction clearly.

inquiry_evidence.quote: A page waits for three independent remote calls. A video encoder performs three expensive calculations. How would you reduce elapsed time in each case, and which case needs more execution capacity?

fundamental_evidence.quote: Repeated waiting requests vs a persistent two-way connection.

application_evidence.quote: Use message direction, frequency, and reconnect behavior to choose.

problem_solved: Select an update transport based on interaction direction, frequency, and recovery requirements rather than a universal faster/slower label.
design_scenario: A frequently interactive editor exchanges updates both ways, while another client can use repeated held requests.
application_steps: State whether messages travel one way or both ways and how frequently they are expected.
Compare a held request that is renewed after each response with a persistent two-way connection.
Define what happens after disconnection, including backoff and recovering missed updates.
Measure active connections, delivery delay, and buffer use.
decision_or_tradeoff: Persistent communication avoids repeated request cycles but adds connection lifecycle and buffering responsibilities; neither transport supplies durable history automatically.
animation_reason: Renewed long-poll requests and persistent bidirectional messages are behaviors over time; the existing real-time communication sequence can illustrate them.

inquiry_evidence.quote: A dashboard receives occasional status changes; an editor exchanges frequent updates in both directions. How would each client learn about new data, and what must happen after disconnection?

fundamental_evidence.quote: Process accumulated records together vs process a continuing flow.

application_evidence.quote: Nightly sales reports favor batches; live fraud signals need timely updates.

problem_solved: Choose processing cadence according to the age of data the business can tolerate and the overhead of processing it.
design_scenario: A shop produces a nightly sales report and also evaluates time-sensitive fraud signals.
application_steps: Specify the maximum acceptable delay separately for the report and the fraud signal.
Accumulate suitable report records for a batch while processing time-sensitive changes continuously.
Define replay and progress tracking so restarts do not lose or double-apply changes.
Measure waiting introduced by batching together with downstream freshness and processing cost.
decision_or_tradeoff: Larger batches can amortize processing overhead but delay results; continuous processing favors freshness while requiring ongoing progress and failure management.
animation_reason: Show identical arriving records waiting for a batch boundary versus entering continuous processing; CDC/replay timing provides a related existing sequence.

inquiry_evidence.quote: Finance needs a complete daily report, while fraud detection must react before a payment decision. Which records would you process together, and where would waiting become unacceptable?

fundamental_evidence.quote: Requests depend on server-local session state vs portable request context.

application_evidence.quote: With an external session store, another app server can handle the next request.

problem_solved: Avoid making a user's next request depend on the same application instance remaining available.
design_scenario: A load balancer routes consecutive shopping-session requests to different application servers.
application_steps: Identify session information that exists only in one application process.
Make required request context portable or place shared session data in a deliberately designed external store.
Route the next request to another instance and verify authorization and session behavior.
Account for availability, freshness, and access costs of the shared state dependency.
decision_or_tradeoff: Stateless application instances simplify replacement and routing, but the system still has durable business state and may depend on shared session infrastructure.
animation_reason: Route the same session first to A and then B, contrasting missing local memory with a shared store; the failure occurs between requests.

inquiry_evidence.quote: Request one reaches server A and stores a login session in its memory. Request two reaches B. How should B identify the user, and what happens when A disappears?

fundamental_evidence.quote: Reads reflect completed writes vs replicas converge after writes stop and communication recovers.

application_evidence.quote: Profile display may tolerate lag; stock reservation needs an explicit correctness rule.

problem_solved: Choose observable data guarantees per operation while defining whether temporary stale reads are acceptable.
design_scenario: A profile display may show an older value, while reserving the last ticket must preserve the no-duplicate-sale invariant.
application_steps: State the operation's correctness invariant and acceptable staleness.
Allow profile reads to use lagging replicas only within the product's policy.
Require an authoritative reservation decision before confirming a sale; define failure behavior when coordination is unavailable.
For eventual behavior, state the convergence assumptions: writes stop, communication recovers, and the replication/reconciliation mechanism can complete.
decision_or_tradeoff: Serving stale values can preserve useful access with less coordination; stronger read guarantees may require waiting or rejecting requests. Eventual consistency requires convergence under its assumptions, not permanent arbitrary staleness.
animation_reason: Show a completed write, a lagging read, and later convergence; contrast with a partition that prevents an authoritative reservation decision.

inquiry_evidence.quote: An address display can be briefly old, but two buyers want the last ticket. What must each read promise, and what should happen when replicas cannot communicate?

fundamental_evidence.quote: The cache loads missed reads vs the cache layer persists writes synchronously.

application_evidence.quote: A product cache can load read misses and synchronously persist writes; these policies can be combined.

problem_solved: Assign cache loading and persistence responsibilities without mistaking complementary read and write policies for mutually exclusive designs.
design_scenario: A product cache loads a price after a read miss, while a write path persists a later price update synchronously.
application_steps: Trace who loads the backing store when a requested price is absent.
Separately trace when a write is considered persisted and acknowledged.
Combine read-through and write-through where the requirements warrant both.
Define concurrent update, failure, and stale-value behavior rather than assuming the combination guarantees perfect freshness.
decision_or_tradeoff: Read-through moves miss-loading responsibility into a layer; write-through adds synchronous persistence work to writes. They solve different sides of access and may coexist.
animation_reason: Separate read-miss arrows from write-and-persist arrows, then overlay both policies in one cache; the existing caching sequence can supply part of this explanation.

inquiry_evidence.quote: A price lookup misses the cache; later, a writer changes the price. Who should fetch the missing record, who should persist the write, and can those responsibilities coexist?

fundamental_evidence.quote: Sender initiates delivery vs receiver requests updates.

application_evidence.quote: A webhook pushes payment news; polling repeatedly asks for it.

problem_solved: Decide who initiates update delivery and how to avoid unnecessary requests or unhandled delivery failures.
design_scenario: A checkout needs payment status from an independent provider.
application_steps: Compare receiving a provider webhook with periodically requesting status.
For push, verify the sender and durably accept events before acknowledgement according to the provider contract.
Handle duplicates and out-of-order events, or define polling frequency and acceptable status delay for pull.
Measure timely business completion rather than only endpoint response speed.
decision_or_tradeoff: Push can avoid repeated empty polls but requires a reachable and recoverable receiver; pull gives the receiver control over requests while introducing polling load and delay.
animation_reason: A provider-initiated webhook compared with repeated receiver-initiated checks makes request ownership and delay visible.

inquiry_evidence.quote: A checkout needs to learn whether an external payment completed. Should it keep asking, or wait for a notification? How would your design recover a missed update?

fundamental_evidence.quote: Resource-oriented interfaces vs calling defined operations.

application_evidence.quote: Use resource reads for products; typed service operations can reserve inventory.

problem_solved: Choose an interface model without assuming it supplies the service's business correctness or storage consistency guarantees.
design_scenario: A shop exposes product resources to clients and an inventory-reservation operation between cooperating services.
application_steps: Identify whether clients primarily manipulate resources or invoke defined service operations.
Specify the product-read or reservation contract, including errors, authorization, and retries.
Keep inventory correctness independent of the interface label and enforce the invariant in the service/data design.
Measure end-to-end backend work rather than choosing solely from a REST-versus-RPC speed stereotype.
decision_or_tradeoff: Resource semantics and typed operation contracts suit different client and service needs; neither automatically selects a consistency model.
animation_reason: A static pair of resource and operation requests, with identical invariant requirements, is sufficient.

inquiry_evidence.quote: One client browses product records while another asks inventory to reserve five units. How would you express each contract, and which interface makes the operation and its failure understandable?

fundamental_evidence.quote: Caller waits for completion vs completion is decoupled from the initiating call.

application_evidence.quote: Queued email can finish after the order confirmation.

problem_solved: Decide which work must finish before responding and which can safely complete later without misrepresenting business state.
design_scenario: A shop confirms an order while an email worker sends its receipt later.
application_steps: Specify what order confirmation guarantees and which email work may remain pending.
Durably record or enqueue the deferred work with recovery for the handoff.
Acknowledge completion at the appropriate stage and make repeated email jobs safe.
Monitor queue age and failure recovery instead of treating a fast initial response as proof that email completed.
decision_or_tradeoff: Deferring work can shorten the initiating request but adds lag, queue state, retry handling, and truthful pending-status requirements.
animation_reason: Show the order response returning before the email worker completes; queue delivery and acknowledgement sequences make the distinction concrete.

inquiry_evidence.quote: An order is committed, but the email provider is slow. What must finish before you respond to the buyer, and how would the remaining work survive a crash?

fundamental_evidence.quote: Time for one operation vs operations completed per unit time.

application_evidence.quote: More counters can serve more customers without shortening each individual checkout.

problem_solved: Avoid confusing increased total capacity with a shorter wait or execution time for each request.
design_scenario: A checkout service adds workers and completes more requests per second, but each successful checkout still takes the same time.
application_steps: Measure per-operation durations and completed operations per interval separately.
Trace the slow request's critical path before optimizing latency.
Add capacity or reduce service work where saturation limits throughput.
Retest under representative load and inspect waiting, tail latency, errors, and the next shared bottleneck.
decision_or_tradeoff: More workers can increase completed requests without shortening individual service time; excessive concurrency can instead increase queuing and tail latency.
animation_reason: A moving sequence can keep each customer's service duration constant while changing how many customers finish in the interval.

inquiry_evidence.quote: Adding workers doubles completed orders per second, yet each buyer waits the same time. What improved, what did not, and which measure matches the complaint you are trying to solve?

fundamental_evidence.quote: Asking questions about the exact scope of the problem, and clarifying functional requirements early in the interview is essential.

problem_solved: Turns an ambiguous design prompt into explicit scope, measurable requirements, defensible architecture, and a reasoned discussion of bottlenecks and failures.
design_scenario: A practice design contains a 200 ms read whose repeated database queries consume 150 ms, so the candidate must justify an optimization rather than add unrelated components.

application_evidence.quote: Suppose a read currently takes 200 ms, with 150 ms spent on repeated database queries. Say what you would measure, propose caching or a query improvement, then explain freshness or write costs.

application_steps: Clarify scope, functional behavior, scale, latency, availability, and failure assumptions.
Estimate with units, define interfaces and data, then draw a complete request path.
Identify one observed bottleneck, propose a change, explain its new costs and failure modes, and compare the same workload before and after.
decision_or_tradeoff: Optimize a demonstrated bottleneck with explicit freshness, write, or failure costs; a queue does not automatically shorten a synchronous database query.
animation_reason: The structured method, timing guide, worked bottleneck example, and worksheet are adequately expressed as static steps; there is no system-state race that requires animation.

inquiry_evidence.quote: “Design chat.” What must you ask before choosing components for a two-person messenger versus a global broadcast service?

fundamental_evidence.quote: A URL shortener service creates an alias or a short URL for a long URL.

problem_solved: Creates unique short aliases and serves high-volume redirects while preserving update, deletion, and abuse rules.
design_scenario: A campaign makes one link viral while a 20,000-redirects/second workload has a 95% cache hit rate; the link owner may later disable that link.

application_evidence.quote: Under these simplified assumptions, database reads fall to about `20,000 × 0.05 = 1,000/second`.

application_steps: Create a mapping while enforcing short-code uniqueness in authoritative storage; retry generation after collisions.
Trace redirect service, cached mapping, database miss, and destination response, keeping acceptable delayed analytics off the critical path.
Measure miss load and viral-key behavior, coalesce simultaneous reloads, and enforce expiry or invalidation needed for edits and disabled links.
decision_or_tradeoff: Local and shared caches reduce redirect and database work but create stale copies; long cache lifetimes can conflict with disabling or editing a link.
animation_reason: Show cache hit and miss request paths, asynchronous analytics, and a disabled viral mapping remaining cached; this connects optimization to full request flow and invalidation correctness.

inquiry_evidence.quote: A campaign needs short links. One link suddenly receives thousands of clicks a second, and its owner must still be able to disable it. Sketch the simplest lookup you would build. Which work must finish before redirecting the visitor? If you keep extra copies of the destination, how will a disabled link stop working?

fundamental_evidence.quote: If the recipient is offline, retain the message for later retrieval.

problem_solved: Provides durable messaging across intermittent connections with explicit accepted, delivered, and read meanings, safe retries, and scalable recipient routing.
design_scenario: A recipient disconnects after message 41 but before acknowledgement, reconnects through another server, and must resume without duplicate visible messages.

application_evidence.quote: Pause a worker after it records a message but before it acknowledges processing. On restart, verify that redelivery does not create a second visible message.

application_steps: Record the message durably before acknowledging the chosen acceptance guarantee, and retain offline-recipient work.
Route to the server holding the current recipient connection, while handling stale connection-location information and reconnects.
Reuse stable message identifiers and enforce deduplication at the durable write, define ordering per conversation, and measure fanout attempts and backlog age.
decision_or_tradeoff: Queueing absorbs bursts but does not add unlimited delivery capacity; conversation-scoped ordering permits parallel chats while global ordering adds coordination and a hot group can dominate work.
animation_reason: Animate accepted versus delivered states, offline storage, lost acknowledgement, repeated delivery, and reconnect to a new connection server so duplicate handling is part of the whole message flow.

inquiry_evidence.quote: A sender presses Send while the recipient is offline. The sender then loses connectivity and presses Send again. What would you promise each person at each point? Where would you keep the message, how would you distinguish a retry from a new message, and what evidence would justify showing a delivered mark?

fundamental_evidence.quote: On a write, store the post durably, then distribute references to the followers' timelines if using precomputed feeds.

problem_solved: Delivers follower feeds with an explicit balance between publication fanout cost, read latency, freshness, and visibility enforcement.
design_scenario: A chronological feed receives 1,000 posts/second with 300 followers per post, while a celebrity post creates a much larger fanout burst and some distribution workers lag.

application_evidence.quote: One option is a mixed strategy: distribute ordinary authors' posts ahead of time, while merging very large authors' posts when a follower reads the feed.

application_steps: Store each post durably and decide whether follower timelines are precomputed references or assembled on reads.
Estimate timeline insertions per post and compare ordinary versus celebrity workloads before choosing a mixed fanout strategy.
Paginate and cache with correct visibility context, monitor post-to-feed lag, and enforce deletion or privacy rules even when old references remain.
decision_or_tradeoff: Precomputed feeds make reads cheaper but amplify writes and lag; merging large authors at read time reduces massive write bursts while making reads perform additional work.
animation_reason: Show publication, queued timeline fanout, delayed projection, and a follower read that merges a large-author path; then show why a deleted post reference must not expose content.

inquiry_evidence.quote: One account has 20 followers; another has 20 million. Both publish a post. Readers expect their home feeds quickly. Would you prepare every follower’s feed when a post is written, or assemble it when someone opens the app? Follow the work and storage costs for each account before choosing.

fundamental_evidence.quote: A rendition is one encoded version, such as a particular resolution and bitrate.

problem_solved: Prepares durable video variants and serves repeated media segments efficiently without placing encoding or large media transfers on the playback API path.
design_scenario: A new title launches into cold regional caches while 2,000 concurrent viewers request roughly 4 megabits/second each.

application_evidence.quote: Cache reusable segments near viewers through a CDN. A warm popular segment can serve many viewers without each request reaching origin storage.

application_steps: Store an upload and generate renditions in retry-safe background jobs; publish usable manifests only when required outputs are ready.
Trace playback manifest and media-segment requests separately from login and application APIs.
Use regionally reusable segments and appropriate cache keys, choose renditions for device and network conditions, and measure startup delay, buffering, quality, and origin traffic under cold caches.
decision_or_tradeoff: More renditions improve adaptation while increasing encoding and storage; lower bitrates can reduce buffering at a quality cost, and warm-cache success does not establish cold-launch origin capacity.
animation_reason: Animate upload-to-rendition preparation independently of manifest/segment playback, with CDN hits and cold misses; show that adding login servers does not remove media bandwidth demand.

inquiry_evidence.quote: A viewer on a weak mobile connection and another on a fast TV connection select the same film. A million other viewers may join tonight. How would you prepare, locate, and deliver the bytes each player needs? What changes when bandwidth drops halfway through playback, and which work could have happened before anyone pressed Play?

fundamental_evidence.quote: Candidate discovery does not reserve a driver.

problem_solved: Finds suitably fresh nearby candidates and assigns a limited driver resource without letting simultaneous requests create conflicting assignments.
design_scenario: Two passengers discover the same driver while location reports may be delayed, and a 100,000-driver fleet changes reporting frequency from five seconds to one second.

application_evidence.quote: Use an atomic conditional update or another explicit coordination mechanism to move a driver from available to assigned.

application_steps: Index observed driver locations with timestamps and query neighboring spatial cells before checking exact distance and freshness.
Apply a conditional available-to-assigned transition to the selected candidate; if it fails, choose another candidate rather than trust the earlier search.
Tune update intervals and partitioning against observed movement, freshness needs, hotspot load, and matching latency; rehearse delayed updates and assignment timeouts.
decision_or_tradeoff: Fresher updates increase bandwidth and write load; finer cells or partitions reduce some candidate work but add lookups and boundary coordination, and approximate discovery cannot replace authoritative assignment.
animation_reason: Animate location update, neighboring-cell discovery, two simultaneous passenger selections, and the atomic assignment where only one wins; include stale locations and retrying another candidate.

inquiry_evidence.quote: A rider requests a trip near a map-cell boundary. Two riders can see the same nearby driver, whose last location is already several seconds old. How would you find candidates without missing a driver across the boundary? What must happen before you promise either rider that this driver is theirs?
